rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Capacitors combine in two ways. **Series** (end-to-end): each carries the same induced charge Q while voltages add, giving $\frac{1}{C_s} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2}$ — equivalent capacitance *smaller than the smallest*, but withstanding higher total voltage. **Parallel** (same two nodes): each sees the same V while charges add, giving $C_p = C_1 + C_2$ — larger than the largest, storing more charge.…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - Series: 1/C_s = Σ1/Cᵢ; two: C₁C₂/(C₁+C₂) - Parallel: C_p = ΣCᵢ

rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Series capacitors: same Q, divided V. Parallel: same V, divided Q** — the exact mirror of resistors.  ·  **Series C is smaller than the smallest member.**

rows.label: Special cases
rows.text: "In series the charge is the same on each capacitor; in parallel the potential difference is the same."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***NEB 2024*** — 2 μF and 3 μF: series 1.2 μF, parallel 5 μF.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Wiring Capacitors Together Capacitors in series divide the voltage; in parallel they share the charge. Their combination rules run *opposite* to resistors', and NEB 2024 tested both in one 3-mark numerical.  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts (NEB 2024) ### 2.1 Series combination Capacitors end to end carry the **same charge** Q (induced plate by plate); voltages add: $$V = V_1 + V_2 = \frac{Q}{C_1} + \frac{Q}{C_2} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{C_s} = \frac{1}{C_1} + \frac{1}{C_2}$$ — the equivalent capacitance is **smaller than the smallest**; series withstands higher total voltage.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: "Two in series: C = C₁C₂/(C₁+C₂) — product over sum."

rows.label: Board question
rows.text: **Numerical (3m): 2, 3 and 6 μF in parallel; find C and the charge on the 3 μF at 10 V.** — C_p = 11 μF; Q₃ = 3 μF × 10 V = 30 μC.

rows.label: Hints
rows.text: Quote the comparison with resistors if asked conceptually.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: **Capacitor rules are resistor rules inverted** — a classic conceptual trap.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Series stacking lets capacitors survive higher voltages — each takes only its share.
